reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with recurrent episodes resembling mechanical bowel obstruction, with distension, pain, vomiting and altered bowel habit, but no obstructing lesion is found
Diagnosis requires imaging showing dilated bowel with air-fluid levels while excluding a mechanical cause, sometimes needing repeated investigation
It reflects a failure of effective propulsion from disease of the enteric nerves (neuropathic), smooth muscle (myopathic) or interstitial cells of Cajal
May be primary or secondary to systemic disorders such as systemic sclerosis, diabetes, amyloidosis, paraneoplastic syndromes or mitochondrial disease
Chronic stasis predisposes to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, worsening malabsorption and diarrhoea
Many patients become dependent on nutritional support and are at risk of complications from long-term parenteral nutrition
Management is largely supportive with nutrition, prokinetics, treatment of bacterial overgrowth and avoidance of unnecessary surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction is a severe motility disorder in which the bowel behaves as though obstructed despite the absence of any mechanical blockage. It arises from dysfunction of the neuromuscular apparatus that generates coordinated propulsion, and is classified as neuropathic when the enteric nervous system is affected, myopathic when the intestinal smooth muscle is abnormal, or mesenchymopathic when the interstitial cells of Cajal are deficient. It may be idiopathic or secondary to systemic diseases including connective-tissue disorders, endocrine and metabolic disease, amyloidosis, paraneoplastic processes and mitochondrial cytopathies. Ineffective peristalsis causes luminal stasis, bowel dilatation, bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption.
additionalDifferentials: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth from other causes
Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive disorders
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging and contrast studies to exclude mechanical obstruction
Gastrointestinal transit and, where available, manometric studies to characterise dysmotility
Full-thickness biopsy in selected cases to define neuropathic versus myopathic disease
Screening for secondary causes such as connective-tissue disease, diabetes and amyloid
Breath testing or empirical assessment for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
redFlags: Signs suggesting bowel ischaemia or perforation during an acute episode
Progressive malnutrition and dependence on parenteral nutrition
Line-related sepsis or thrombosis in patients on long-term parenteral nutrition
New or worsening symptoms suggesting an evolving mechanical cause
reference.prognosis: The disorder is typically chronic and often progressive, with significant morbidity from malnutrition, recurrent hospital admissions and complications of nutritional support; prognosis depends on the extent of gut involvement and any underlying systemic disease.
pitfalls: Subjecting patients to repeated futile surgery in search of a mechanical obstruction
Overlooking bacterial overgrowth as a driver of symptoms
Underestimating nutritional requirements and delaying appropriate support
